# Bhisajātaka (Ja 488)

**ID:** Ja 488
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Bhisajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** A Meal of Lotus Fibres
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja488
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul13.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bhisajātaka* (Ja 488) is a canonical Jātaka tale set at Jetavana, delivered by the Buddha concerning a monk who had backslidden because of desire; the Buddha recounts a previous life wherein virtuous ascetics outside the dispensation swore solemn oaths to repudiate sensual temptations [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta entered the forest with six brothers, a sister, a friend, a servant, and a maidservant, living on daily gathered lotus rhizomes or stalks (*bhisa*) [Bareau; Cunningham 1879]. To test the Bodhisatta's modesty and purity, the god Sakka causes the lotus stalks to vanish, prompting the hermits to clear themselves of suspicion by solemnly cursing whoever stole the food with worldly attachments and sensual indulgence [SuttaCentral; Bareau]. In the concluding identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the companions are identified with key disciples, including Ānanda, Sāriputta, and Moggallāna as the brothers, Uppalavaṇṇā as the sister, Khujjuttarā as the maid, and the householder Citta as the servant [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Fausböll 1887]. In Buddhist doctrinal tradition, the tale serves as a foremost illustration of the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*) [Hazra 1994; WAR YAR MEIN DA 2015].

Textual reuse identified by DharmaNexus links the verses closely with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns the narrative with cross-language parallels, most prominently Āryaśūra’s *Jātakamālā* (Tibetan D4150), whose close literary relationship with the Pali version has been examined by modern scholarship [Silk 2008; DharmaNexus], as well as the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* (D0001-2) and the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, scenes from the narrative—featuring the ascetics, a monkey, an elephant, and the lotus offerings—are depicted in early Buddhist sculptural reliefs at Bharhut [Anderson 1978; Cunningham 1879].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Catuttho bhāgo) (Atk S0513a4) (§3.1–13.4 ↔ §2930–2963); Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0512a) (§18.1–21.4 ↔ §1424–1437)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): སྐྱེས་པའི་རབས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུད། (jātakamāla) (D4150) [bo]; འདུལ་བ་གཞི། (vinayavastu) (D0001-2) [bo]; འཕགས་པ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་དྲན་པ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ། (ārya-saddharmānusmṛtyupasthāna) (D0287-2) [bo]; 雜阿含經 (ZH_T02_0099) [zh]; ཐབས་མཁས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་དྲིན་ལན་བསབ་པའི་མདོ། (D0353) [bo]
